primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
mechanism: Warm-reactive IgG binds erythrocyte surface antigens. Splenic macrophages recognize Fc-coated erythrocytes and partially phagocytose or remove them from the circulation, producing predominantly extravascular hemolysis and microspherocyte formation.
vignette: An adult develops fatigue, jaundice, splenomegaly, anemia, reticulocytosis, and spherocytes. The direct antiglobulin test is positive for IgG on erythrocytes.
lead: Which mechanism most directly accounts for the predominant red-cell destruction in this disorder?
correct: Fc-receptor-mediated clearance of IgG-coated erythrocytes by splenic macrophages
distractors: Complement-mediated intravascular lysis of erythrocytes triggered by cold-reactive IgM
Oxidant-induced denaturation of hemoglobin with Heinz-body formation
Mechanical fragmentation of erythrocytes across platelet-rich microthrombi
Failure of erythrocyte membrane-cytoskeleton anchoring with splenic trapping
distractor_notes: Cold-antibody disease is typically driven by IgM and complement; the stem specifically demonstrates warm IgG coating.
G6PD deficiency causes oxidant-induced Heinz bodies and bite cells rather than an IgG-positive direct antiglobulin test.
Microangiopathic hemolysis produces schistocytes and is not the mechanism of warm AIHA.
Hereditary spherocytosis causes membrane-cytoskeletal instability and is direct-antiglobulin-test negative.
key_expl: Warm AIHA is usually mediated by IgG antibodies that bind erythrocytes at body temperature. Fc receptors on splenic macrophages recognize these coated cells, causing partial phagocytosis and extravascular destruction. Membrane loss during this process produces microspherocytes, explaining why spherocytes can appear in both warm AIHA and hereditary spherocytosis.
objective: Explain warm AIHA as predominantly splenic Fc-mediated extravascular destruction of IgG-coated erythrocytes.
clues: direct antiglobulin test positive for IgG
